title: Bijections and Inverse Functions
short: A function has an inverse exactly when it is one-to-one and onto, and (g ∘ f)⁻¹ = f⁻¹ ∘ g⁻¹.
trouble: Students undo a composition in the order it was applied instead of the reverse order.

blocks.html: In algebra you found inverse functions by swapping $x$ and $y$ and solving. Now we can say exactly when that works, using one-to-one and onto, and how inverses behave when functions are chained.

A function $f : A \to B$ has an inverse $f^{-1} : B \to A$, with $f^{-1}(f(a)) = a$ and $f(f^{-1}(b)) = b$, exactly when $f$ is a bijection. For bijections $f : A \to B$ and $g : B \to C$, $(g \circ f)^{-1} = f^{-1} \circ g^{-1}$: undo the last step first.

Reverse every arrow of $f$. For the reversed arrows to form a function from $B$, each element of $B$ needs exactly one arrow coming back. "At least one" is exactly onto; "at most one" is exactly one-to-one. So the inverse exists precisely for bijections. For the composition, $g \circ f$ means "apply $f$, then $g$." To get back you must peel off $g$ first, then $f$, just as you take off your shoes before your socks.

blocks.name: disc-relation
blocks.cap: A bijection. Press "Reverse the arrows": every element of $B$ has exactly one arrow back, so the reversed arrows form the inverse function. Remove an arrow, or add one, and see the inverse break.

blocks.title: Inverting a formula
blocks.q: Show that $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $f(x) = 3x - 2$, is a bijection, and find $f^{-1}$.
steps: Solve $y = 3x - 2$ for $x$: $x = \frac{y + 2}{3}$. Every real $y$ gives exactly one real $x$, so $f$ is onto and one-to-one.

blocks.title: Undoing a composition
blocks.q: Let $f(x) = 2x + 1$ and $g(x) = x^{3}$ on $\mathbb{R}$. Find $(g \circ f)^{-1}(x)$.
steps: $(g \circ f)(x) = (2x + 1)^{3}$: first double and add $1$, then cube.
Undo in reverse order: first undo the cube, $g^{-1}(x) = \sqrt[3]{x}$; then undo $f$, $f^{-1}(x) = \frac{x - 1}{2}$.

blocks.title: A permutation and its inverse
steps: $f^{-1}(1)$ is the input that $f$ sends to $1$: $f(2) = 1$, so $f^{-1}(1) = 2$.

blocks.html: Undoing a composition in the original order. $(g \circ f)^{-1}$ is not $g^{-1} \circ f^{-1}$; that would try to undo $f$ while $g$'s effect is still on top. In the example, $g^{-1}(f^{-1}(125)) = \sqrt[3]{62}$, which is not $2$. Check by plugging one number through: apply $g \circ f$, then your inverse, and see whether you get the number back.
